case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a person who accesses online video content through a free, advertising-supported website/app is a “consumer” under the Video Privacy Protection Act such that the site’s alleged disclosure of video-viewing information can trigger VPPA liability.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 2710 (Video Privacy Protection Act), specifically § 2710(a)(1) (definition of “consumer”) and related provisions governing disclosure of “personally identifiable information.”
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Salazar argues that he qualifies as a VPPA “consumer” because he is a “subscriber” of 247Sports’ digital video service: he repeatedly accessed and viewed video content through the service and (as alleged) used the site/app in a manner that creates an ongoing relationship typical of subscription-based access. He contends the Sixth Circuit adopted an unduly narrow, paywall-or-formal-registration rule that is inconsistent with the VPPA’s text and purpose, and that in modern digital markets many subscription-like relationships are free and supported by advertising rather than direct payment. He also emphasizes that construing “subscriber” to cover users of free digital video services is necessary to prevent easy circumvention of the VPPA’s privacy protections.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Paramount/247Sports argues Salazar is not a VPPA “consumer” because he neither rented/purchased audio-visual materials nor “subscribed” in the ordinary statutory sense—i.e., he did not enter into a continuing commitment or ongoing, account-based relationship that makes him a customer of a video service provider. Respondent defends the Sixth Circuit’s approach as consistent with statutory text and administrable boundaries, warning that petitioner’s broader theory would effectively make nearly any website visitor a “consumer,” dramatically expanding VPPA exposure for publishers and online services and creating substantial compliance and litigation burdens. Respondent further stresses that the VPPA was enacted with specific, transactional video-rental contexts in mind and should not be stretched to cover casual, non-committal access to free online content.
key_precedents: The materials provided do not identify specific Supreme Court precedents by name; the dispute primarily turns on statutory interpretation of the VPPA’s definition of “consumer,” and (in lower courts generally) VPPA cases often revolve around what constitutes a “subscriber” and what qualifies as “personally identifiable information.”

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that the VPPA does not expressly require payment or a formal account, and Yershov illustrates that some nonpaying users can still be “subscribers.” But as Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson emphasize, treating persistent identifiers and repeat access—tracking imposed unilaterally by the provider—as the equivalent of subscription would collapse “subscriber” into “user,” untethering the term from its statutory neighbors (“renter” and “purchaser”) and the parallel “rental, sale, or delivery” framing in § 2710(a)(4). Ellis supplies an administrable boundary consistent with judicial restraint: absent some affirmative, ongoing tie (enrollment-like conduct, account features, or comparable commitment), these allegations do not plausibly plead “subscriber” status. Congress’s decision to adjust consent procedures without expanding “consumer” reinforces, for me, a minimalist holding limited to users who neither register nor otherwise undertake a continuing relationship with the provider.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that the VPPA nowhere expressly requires payment or a formal account and that Yershov treats persistent identifiers plus repeat access as enough, but that functional approach risks substituting modern tracking realities for the statutory term Congress enacted. Read in its textual setting, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch that “subscriber” must take meaning from its neighbors (“renter” and “purchaser”) and the parallel provider-side language (“rental, sale, or delivery”), which together denote an affirmative, continuing relationship rather than passive, free viewing that a provider can unilaterally monitor. Yershov, even if plausible on its own facts, cannot override the ordinary 1988 public meaning and would effectively collapse “subscriber” into “viewer,” expanding liability beyond the administrable boundary reflected in Ellis. If Congress wishes to reach all tracked viewers of free online video, it may amend the definition of “consumer,” but our role is to apply the text as written and originally understood.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Yershov and the VPPA’s remedial purpose is the most serious push, but it ultimately asks us to treat provider-imposed tracking identifiers as the functional equivalent of a user’s affirmative subscription—collapsing “subscriber” into “viewer,” which Congress did not enact. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the administrability consequences are not merely policy worries; they expose the textual problem that a persistent cookie would convert vast swaths of ordinary web traffic into “consumers,” untethered from the statute’s transactional framing (“renter, purchaser, or subscriber” paired with “rental, sale, or delivery”). Ellis supplies the better text-faithful limiting principle: absent some user-initiated, ongoing relationship (enrollment-like conduct, account, or comparable commitment), Salazar has not plausibly alleged he is a VPPA “consumer.” Yershov, even if correct on its facts, is distinguishable to the extent it involved an app-like exchange and functionality closer to affirmative enrollment; it does not compel stretching “subscriber” to cover passive repeat visits here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability point is the most serious counterweight, but it assumes petitioner’s position would treat any tracked visitor as a “subscriber”; I would require an ongoing, user-specific relationship evidenced by repeat access tied to persistent identifiers that the provider uses to deliver the video service in a continuing way, not a one-off anonymous view. Justice Kagan’s proposed “account-based commitment” reads a formality into § 2710(a)(1) that Congress did not enact; “subscriber” can include ad-supported, continuing-access arrangements where the provider recognizes and repeatedly serves the same user, even without payment or registration. The contextual/noscitur-a-sociis argument pressed by Justice Thomas and reinforced through Ellis is helpful as a caution against boundless “user” theories, but it does not compel a registration-or-payment boundary; “subscriber” is the residual category meant to capture non-renter/non-purchaser ongoing relationships, and modern practices can create those relationships through persistent identifiers. Yershov remains persuasive in showing how digital services can create subscriber-like relationships without traditional accounts, and a rigid account requirement would invite easy circumvention of a remedial privacy statute affecting ordinary, vulnerable users with little meaningful notice or bargaining power.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Congress did not write a payment-or-formal-registration requirement and that, as Yershov suggests, modern services can create ongoing relationships through persistent identifiers and repeat access. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively show why that functional move risks detaching “subscriber” from its statutory neighbors (“renter” and “purchaser”) and from the provider-side focus on “rental, sale, or delivery,” effectively collapsing the statute’s threshold into “tracked viewer.” Justice Jackson’s emphasis that the relationship must be “from” the provider—something plausibly rooted in user-initiated enrollment-like conduct or provider-conferred benefits—reinforces my view that unilateral tracking alone is not an administrable textual boundary. Yershov may indicate payment is unnecessary, but it does not compel treating passive, ad-supported repeat viewing without any affirmative undertaking as a “subscription” under § 2710(a)(1).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that “subscriber” need not entail payment or a formal account and that modern services can create continuing relationships through identifiers; but that argument effectively lets unilateral tracking substitute for the affirmative, ongoing relationship the term conveyed in 1988, especially alongside “renter” and “purchaser.” As the Chief Justice notes, using persistent identifiers as the touchstone risks collapsing “subscriber” into “user,” sweeping in ordinary, open-access website visitors and erasing the statute’s limiting threshold. Yershov may show one plausible digital-era application, but—consistent with Justice Kagan’s contextual reading and Ellis’s limiting principle—it is not compelled by the VPPA’s text and would move us from interpretation to updating. The circumvention concern is real policy, yet under separation-of-powers principles the remedy lies with Congress, not an atextual expansion of “subscriber.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the circumvention concern: modern services can create a continuing, identifiable relationship through persistent identifiers and repeat viewing, as Yershov suggests, even without payment. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan correctly note that treating tracking-imposed identifiers as “subscription” collapses “subscriber” into “viewer,” untethering § 2710(a)(1) from its 1988 context alongside “renter” and “purchaser” and creating sweeping, hard-to-administer liability for ordinary open-access browsing. Ellis reinforces that we need some affirmative, user-initiated, ongoing tie—account enrollment, login, or comparable commitment—rather than a relationship the provider can unilaterally manufacture via cookies or device IDs. Under my institutionalist approach, the narrower, administrable reading better respects precedent and statutory continuity while leaving any broader modernization to Congress.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that “subscriber” need not entail payment or formal registration and that persistent identifiers plus repeat access can approximate an ongoing relationship (as in Yershov). But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, reading “subscriber” to arise from tracking that the provider can impose unilaterally risks collapsing the statutory threshold into “viewer,” untethered from the contextual company it keeps with “renter” and “purchaser” in § 2710(a)(1) and the parallel “rental, sale, or delivery” framing in § 2710(a)(4). Yershov does not undermine that contextual, original-public-meaning reading because its app-based allegations look more like enrollment-like exchange and functionality, whereas here the complaint lacks any affirmative undertaking or account-like arrangement “from” the provider. Ellis, as Justice Jackson notes, supplies a workable line consistent with the text: absent allegations of an affirmative, continuing relationship, repeated free access plus identifiers is not enough to plead “subscriber” status.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that the VPPA’s remedial purpose and Yershov caution against a paywall-or-registration bright line, and I agree we should not constitutionalize 1988 business models. But her functional test—persistent identifiers plus repeat access—still risks collapsing “subscriber” into “viewer,” because the provider (or third parties) can unilaterally create that “relationship” without any user-side undertaking, raising the administrability and procedural-fairness concerns Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize. Ellis remains persuasive that § 2710(a)(1) demands some affirmative, ongoing tie “from” the provider—enrollment-like conduct, access privileges, or reciprocal commitments—beyond ordinary free consumption. Congress’s later amendments adjusting consent mechanisms without expanding “consumer” reinforce restraint in stretching “subscriber” on this record, so I would hold the allegations here insufficient.

John Roberts.reasoning: The VPPA defines a “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1). Giving “subscriber” its ordinary meaning at the time of enactment, as this Court instructs for undefined statutory terms, counsels against treating a casual user of a free, ad-supported website/app as a “subscriber” absent some continuing, account-based commitment; an expansive reading risks sweeping in nearly any website visitor and dramatically enlarging liability beyond administrable bounds. Taniguchi v. Kan Pac. Saipan, Ltd., 566 U.S. 560, 566 (2012), reflects the Court’s reluctance to adopt broad constructions of ordinary terms that create wide-ranging consequences, and a narrower construction here also better preserves predictable lines for Congress, courts, and regulated entities. On this record, I would affirm that merely accessing free online videos, without more, does not make the user a VPPA “consumer” under § 2710(a)(1).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under the VPPA’s text, a “consumer” is a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” of a video tape service provider’s “goods or services.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1). Read in its 1988 public meaning and in context with the statute’s parallel “rental, sale, or delivery” language defining the provider, § 2710(a)(4), “subscriber” connotes an account-based, continuing relationship—typically involving a commitment (often payment) for ongoing delivery—rather than mere repeat access to free, advertising-supported content. Expanding “subscriber” to include any user who watches free videos would sever the term from its statutory companions (“renter” and “purchaser”) and effectively extend VPPA liability beyond the limited, transaction-focused regime Congress enacted. Because Salazar alleges only casual access to free online content without the kind of subscription relationship the statute contemplates, he is not a “consumer” under § 2710(a)(1).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2710(a)(1) defines a “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider,” and read in its ordinary 1988 sense and in context, “subscriber” connotes a continuing, account-based commitment—typically involving affirmative enrollment and often payment—rather than mere repeated, free viewing of ad-supported content. The statutory structure reinforces that reading: “renter/purchaser/subscriber” in § 2710(a)(1) parallels “rental/sale/delivery” in § 2710(a)(4), indicating Congress targeted transactional or ongoing service relationships, not casual site visitors. Expanding “subscriber” to include anyone who repeatedly accesses free online videos would erase administrable limits, dramatically broaden VPPA exposure for publishers, and invite abusive litigation far beyond the statute’s video-rental context. Because Salazar alleged only free access without the kind of ongoing subscription relationship the text contemplates, he is not a VPPA “consumer” and the complaint fails at the threshold.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The VPPA defines “consumer” to include any “subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1), and nothing in that text requires payment or a formal video-specific “account” as a precondition to subscriber status. Consistent with Yershov v. Gannett, 820 F.3d 482, 487–89 (1st Cir. 2016), a user who repeatedly accesses a provider’s video service through an app/site in a way that creates an ongoing, identifiable relationship (including through persistent identifiers) can qualify as a “subscriber,” particularly where a contrary rule would permit easy circumvention of Congress’s privacy protections. Ellis v. Cartoon Network, 803 F.3d 1251, 1256–57 (11th Cir. 2015), properly rejects treating a purely anonymous, one-off viewer as a subscriber, but it does not justify a rigid paywall-or-registration requirement that fails to account for modern ad-supported subscription-like relationships. Interpreting “subscriber” to include such users best effectuates the VPPA’s remedial purpose of protecting ordinary people—often unaware of tracking—from disclosure of sensitive viewing information, while leaving courts to police administrable limits by requiring a meaningful ongoing relationship rather than mere casual browsing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The VPPA defines a “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1). Read in statutory context—alongside the provider definition focused on “rental, sale, or delivery” of “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” § 2710(a)(4)—“subscriber” most naturally connotes an ongoing, account-based commitment (the demand-side analogue to ongoing “delivery”), not a person who merely views free, ad-supported videos without registration or any continuing obligation. That construction gives administrable boundaries and avoids effectively turning “any” visitor into a “consumer,” while still covering modern subscription-like relationships where the user affirmatively establishes continuing access (e.g., accounts, logins, or recurring arrangements). Because Salazar alleges only repeated access to free content without the kind of continuing relationship that makes him a “subscriber,” he is not a “consumer” for purposes of § 2710(b)(1).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The VPPA defines a “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1). Read in context and according to ordinary public meaning in 1988, “subscriber” connotes a continuing, account- or payment-based commitment for delivery over time, and it fits alongside “renter” and “purchaser” as part of a transactional triad; mere free, ad-supported viewing without any such commitment does not. The statute’s parallel structure reinforces this: a “video tape service provider” is engaged in the “rental, sale, or delivery” of audio-visual materials, § 2710(a)(4), and the consumer-side terms should be interpreted to match those supply-side concepts rather than expand “subscriber” to include virtually any website visitor. Expanding liability by updating “subscriber” to modern digital usage would be a policy choice for Congress, not this Court, particularly given separation-of-powers concerns about courts effectively rewriting statutory thresholds for private damages actions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the VPPA, a protected “consumer” is one who “rents, purchases, or subscribes to goods or services from a video tape service provider.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1). Read in its 1988 statutory context and ordinary meaning, “subscribe” connotes a continuing, account-based commitment—typically involving an affirmative enrollment (and often advance, recurring payment)—and it appears in a limiting triad (“rent,” “purchase,” or “subscribe”) that indicates Congress meant to cover transactional or commitment-based relationships rather than casual, open-access viewing. Extending “subscriber” to anyone who repeatedly watches free, advertising-supported videos without registration risks turning ordinary website visitors into “consumers,” creating an unworkable and expansive regime not clearly chosen by Congress and raising serious institutional and administrability concerns. Absent a clearer textual hook, judicial restraint and respect for history and tradition counsel leaving any modernization of the VPPA’s scope to Congress rather than judicial expansion through an atextual reading of “subscriber.”

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under the VPPA, a “consumer” is “any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1). Read in its ordinary 1988 sense and in the company of “renter” and “purchaser,” “subscriber” most naturally denotes a person who enters into an ongoing, account-based relationship or continuing commitment for the provider’s goods or services, not a member of the public who merely returns to a free, advertising-supported site to view content. Petitioner’s broader construction risks collapsing the statutory boundary by converting essentially any repeat website visitor into a “consumer,” a result difficult to square with the statute’s text and administrable limits, especially given Congress’s focus on transactional video-rental contexts when enacting § 2710. Absent a clearer statutory hook showing that free access alone creates a subscriber relationship “from” the provider, I would affirm the narrower reading and vote for Respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The VPPA defines a “consumer” as “any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1), and the ordinary meaning of “subscriber” implies an affirmative, ongoing relationship (typically account-based or otherwise involving a continuing commitment) rather than mere repeated viewing of free, ad-supported content. Consistent with Ellis v. Cartoon Network, Inc., 803 F.3d 1251 (11th Cir. 2015), Congress chose not to use broader terms like “user” or “viewer,” including when it updated the statute’s consent mechanisms in 2012–2013 without expanding “consumer,” which counsels against extending liability to essentially any website visitor. A broader rule would create serious administrability and fairness concerns—risking VPPA coverage for casual, non-committal access and inviting sweeping litigation exposure untethered to the kind of transactional relationship the statute targets. On this record, absent allegations of a true subscription relationship to audiovisual materials (e.g., registration, account features, or commitments tied to video access), Salazar is not plausibly a “consumer” under § 2710(a)(1).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a person who downloaded and used the free 247Sports mobile app—without paying money—qualifies as a “consumer” under the Video Privacy Protection Act such that disclosure of his video-viewing information can trigger liability.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 2710 (Video Privacy Protection Act), especially § 2710(a)(1) (definition of “consumer”) and related provisions governing disclosure of “personally identifiable information.”
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Salazar argues that he is a “consumer” because the VPPA’s definition covers not only renters or purchasers, but also “subscriber[s]” of a provider’s goods or services, and modern app users are subscribers when they sign up for, obtain ongoing access to, and use an app-based video service (even if it is free). He contends the Sixth Circuit adopted an unduly narrow, payment-focused understanding of “subscriber” that is inconsistent with the statutory text, Congress’s privacy-protective purpose, and the realities of today’s ad-supported digital video ecosystem. He further maintains that construing “subscriber” to require payment or a formal paid relationship would gut the VPPA for the most common contemporary mode of video distribution (free apps funded by advertising and data), undermining Congress’s intent to prevent disclosure of individuals’ video-viewing choices.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Paramount/247Sports argues that Salazar is not a “consumer” because he neither rented nor purchased videos and did not have the kind of ongoing, committed relationship that makes someone a “subscriber” as the statute uses that term. In its view, simply downloading and using a free app (and receiving content) is not enough; otherwise almost any casual viewer would become a “subscriber,” dramatically expanding VPPA exposure beyond what Congress contemplated in 1988. Respondent emphasizes administrable limits and warns that an expansive interpretation would transform routine online data flows and ordinary analytics/advertising practices into high-stakes VPPA litigation, imposing heavy costs on publishers and tech companies and chilling digital media offerings.
key_precedents: The Sixth Circuit decision below in Salazar v. Paramount Global (d/b/a 247Sports) (case under review)
Ellis v. Cartoon Network, Inc. (11th Cir.) (interpreting “subscriber” under the VPPA in the context of a free app)
Yershov v. Gannett Satellite Information Network, Inc. (1st Cir.) (VPPA coverage for app users / disclosure of identifiers)
In re Nickelodeon Consumer Privacy Litigation (3d Cir.) (VPPA interpretation and limits on “personally identifiable information”)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson offer the strongest counter: § 2710(a)(1) contains no payment requirement and a “continuing affiliation/persistent identifier” test might avoid equating every viewer with a consumer. But even accepting that premise, on these pleadings there is no account, registration, recurring delivery, or other enrollment-like commitment, so the relationship still looks like the transitory access Ellis treated as insufficient, and adopting petitioner’s broader “data-for-service” theory risks collapsing Congress’s renter/purchaser/subscriber triad into “any user” in a statutory-damages regime. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Yershov usefully highlights the circuit split and shows that some app relationships can be subscription-like when tied to identifiable, ongoing access, but it does not supply a textual hook to extend “subscriber” to ordinary free app use absent concrete indicia of commitment. I would therefore affirm narrowly: Salazar has not plausibly alleged he was a “subscriber” here, leaving room for different facts (account-based or otherwise enrollment-like app relationships) in a future case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s “continuing affiliation/persistent identifier” approach is the strongest petitioner-side limiting principle, but under the original public meaning in 1988—especially in the narrowing triad “renter, purchaser, or subscriber”—“subscriber” connotes an affirmative, enrollment-like commitment to receive a continuing service, not ordinary free app use with passive background data flows. Justice Sotomayor is right that the statute does not require payment, and I do not impose a money-only rule; the problem is that petitioners’ test effectively converts “subscriber” into “user,” collapsing Congress’s chosen limitation and expanding a statutory-damages regime without clear textual warrant. Yershov, as Justice Jackson notes, may fit cases with more account-like indicia of durable, identified affiliation, but it does not displace Ellis’s administrable distinction where the allegations lack registration, an account, recurring delivery, or other concrete commitment. On these pleadings, I would adhere to the statute’s text as originally understood and affirm.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that § 2710(a)(1) omits any payment requirement and that ad-supported apps can involve a continuing affiliation—does not answer the textual question of what “subscriber” meant in 1988, especially placed alongside “renter” and “purchaser.” As the Chief Justice stresses, their “ongoing relationship/persistent identifier” approach risks collapsing the triad into “any user,” with sweeping statutory-damages consequences, and it does so by treating routine app use plus passive data transmission as subscription-like without the affirmative, enrollment-type commitment Ellis found lacking. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Yershov highlights a split and shows that some app arrangements might plausibly be “subscription-like,” but Yershov’s broader “data-as-consideration” framing would effectively modernize the term beyond its ordinary meaning; on these pleaded facts (no registration, account, or comparable undertaking), I would not extend the statute. I therefore remain with Respondent on the narrow ground that Salazar has not plausibly alleged he was a “subscriber.”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’ administrability warning is the strongest point for Respondent, and I agree we must avoid turning “subscriber” into “any viewer,” especially in a statutory-damages regime. But as Justice Kagan explains, the textual limiter need not be payment or formal registration; it can be indicia of an ongoing affiliation—here alleged through continued app-based access coupled with persistent identification and targeted disclosure—so we do not rewrite Congress’s term into “paying subscriber.” Justice Thomas and Justice Alito lean on Ellis, yet Ellis is best read to reject purely transitory, noncommittal access; it does not mandate an account-or-money requirement in every modern app setting where continuity and identification are plausibly alleged. Given the VPPA’s remedial privacy purpose and the pleaded facts, I would not foreclose coverage at the threshold and would allow the “subscriber” question to develop past the motion-to-dismiss stage.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s administrability concern—that treating every free app user as a “subscriber” collapses the renter/purchaser/subscriber triad—is the strongest point on the other side, and I agree we need a limiting principle. But I remain unpersuaded by Chief Justice Roberts’ and Justice Kavanaugh’s move to make “registration/account/recurring obligation” the decisive proxies, because § 2710(a)(1) contains no such terms and Ellis is better read as rejecting transitory, noncommittal access—not as imposing a categorical enrollment requirement. My limiter stays textual and workable: a plaintiff must plausibly allege ongoing affiliation/continuity with the service (here, app-based access plus allegations of persistent identification tied to that access), which gives “subscriber” independent meaning without turning it into “user.” Yershov, while not controlling, reinforces that app-based relationships can be subscription-like when they involve continuing, identified access, and at the pleading stage these allegations are enough to proceed without deciding the outer boundary.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that § 2710(a)(1) nowhere says a subscriber must pay, and that administrability alone cannot justify rewriting the statute; I agree we cannot smuggle in a payment requirement. But their “continuing affiliation/persistent identifier” approach still risks updating “subscriber” to fit modern data-monetization rather than applying the ordinary public meaning Congress enacted in 1988, especially given the narrowing triad “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” which connotes an affirmative, enrollment-like commitment. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Yershov usefully shows that some app relationships can be subscription-like, yet that case turns on more concrete account-like indicia than the complaint alleges here and cannot erase the textual inference (as the Chief Justice stresses) that Congress chose “subscriber” instead of “user.” In a statutory-damages regime, any close call should be resolved by hewing to the narrower term Congress used, leaving broader modernization to Congress.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that § 2710(a)(1) contains no payment requirement and that ad-supported apps can create continuing, data-driven relationships; I agree we cannot rewrite “subscriber” to mean “paying subscriber.” But Chief Justice Roberts is right that their “continuing affiliation/persistent identifier” test, at least on these pleadings, risks collapsing “subscriber” into “any user,” especially given the narrowing triad “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” and Congress’s decision not to expand that triad when it amended consent in 2012. Yershov (as Justice Jackson stresses) matters because it shows an app can be subscription-like, yet it also featured more concrete, account-like indicia of an ongoing, identified relationship than alleged here, making Ellis’s administrable line the better fit for a statutory-damages regime. Absent allegations of registration, account enrollment, or comparable commitment, I would affirm that Salazar has not plausibly alleged he was a “subscriber.”

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s “indicia of continuing affiliation” test is the strongest petitioner-side proposal because it seeks an administrable limit without inserting a payment requirement, and Justice Sotomayor is right that § 2710(a)(1) does not demand money. But under the original public meaning of “subscriber” in 1988—especially in the narrowing triad “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” as the Chief Justice emphasizes—there must be some affirmative, subscription-like undertaking (enrollment, account, registration, or comparable commitment) beyond mere download-and-use plus passive identifiers. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Yershov underscores that some app relationships can be subscription-like when tied to identifiable, account-like continuity, yet on these pleaded facts that linkage is not adequately alleged and expanding “subscriber” to cover routine free app use risks collapsing the statutory term into “user” in a statutory-damages regime. I therefore would affirm on the limited ground that Salazar has not plausibly alleged he was a “subscriber” here, leaving harder app/account cases for a record that actually shows subscription-like indicia.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern—echoed by Justices Kavanaugh and Barrett—that reading “subscriber” to include routine free-app use would collapse the renter/purchaser/subscriber triad into “any user” is the strongest point for Respondent, but I do not think the proper judicial response is to graft a registration/payment/enrollment prerequisite onto § 2710(a)(1) that Congress did not write. Justice Kagan’s “continuing affiliation” limiter answers the collapse problem in a more text-faithful way: it excludes fleeting, transitory viewing while still giving “subscriber” work to do where the complaint plausibly alleges an ongoing app-based relationship tied to persistent identifiers. Ellis v. Cartoon Network, as Justices Thomas and Gorsuch stress, is best read to reject bare, momentary access without meaningful connection; it does not compel a categorical rule that app users cannot be subscribers absent formal enrollment, especially at the pleading stage. Given the VPPA’s privacy-protective purpose and the statute’s choice to include “subscriber” distinct from “purchaser,” I would allow these allegations to proceed rather than foreclose coverage as a matter of law.

John Roberts.reasoning: The VPPA defines “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1); reading “subscriber” to include any person who merely downloads and uses a free app without a continuing, committed relationship risks converting ordinary viewing into subscription and greatly expanding liability beyond the statute’s administrable bounds. Consistent with Ellis v. Cartoon Network, Inc., 803 F.3d 1251 (11th Cir. 2015), Congress could have used broader terms like “user” or “viewer” (and did not), and its later amendments did not expand the definition of “consumer,” counseling caution and a narrow construction that preserves institutional legitimacy and avoids disruptive consequences. While petitioner argues that disclosure of data in an ad-supported ecosystem should qualify, that policy judgment is better left to Congress, particularly given the VPPA’s detailed consent regime and the risk of sweeping in routine analytics practices. On these narrow grounds, Salazar’s free-app use without more does not make him a “subscriber” under § 2710(a)(1), so he is not a “consumer” entitled to sue under the Act.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying the statute’s text as enacted, § 2710(a)(1) limits “consumer” to a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” of a provider’s goods or services, and “subscriber” in ordinary 1988 usage connotes an affirmative, ongoing commitment to receive a continuing service—not mere passive access to freely available content. Reading “subscriber” to include anyone who downloads and uses a free app would effectively rewrite Congress’s narrower terms (“subscriber”) into broader ones (“user” or “viewer”), a move inconsistent with textualism and the administrable limits the definition supplies. The Eleventh Circuit’s analysis in Ellis v. Cartoon Network appropriately reflects that ordinary meaning, rejecting VPPA coverage where the plaintiff simply used a free app without the kind of ongoing, subscription-like relationship the statute presupposes. Congress’s later amendments addressed online consent mechanisms without expanding “consumer,” reinforcing that courts should not enlarge liability beyond the text of § 2710(a)(1).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2710(a)(1) defines a “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services,” and the ordinary meaning of “subscriber” connotes an ongoing, committed relationship rather than a casual user of freely available content. As Ellis v. Cartoon Network, Inc., 803 F.3d 1251 (11th Cir. 2015), reasoned, Congress could have used broader terms like “user” or “viewer” (either in 1988 or when it amended the VPPA in 2012 to modernize consent) but did not, counseling against extending “subscriber” to every free-app downloader. Reading “subscriber” to cover anyone who downloads and uses a free app would effectively treat nearly all digital visitors as VPPA “consumers,” producing an unadministrable and expansive liability regime inconsistent with the statute’s text and the practical limits Congress appears to have chosen. Accordingly, Salazar’s unpaid use of the 247Sports app, without more indicia of subscription-like commitment, does not trigger VPPA coverage as a “consumer” under § 2710(a)(1).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The VPPA defines a “consumer” to include not only “any renter or purchaser” but also “any subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1), and nothing in that text makes payment a prerequisite to being a “subscriber.” In a modern ad-supported app ecosystem, users frequently exchange valuable consideration in the form of persistent identifiers and data for ongoing access to audiovisual content; reading “subscriber” to require money would sharply narrow the statute and undermine Congress’s privacy-protective purpose. The First Circuit in Yershov v. Gannett recognized that app-based users can plausibly qualify as “consumers” under the VPPA where the relationship entails ongoing access and the transmission of identifying information tied to video viewing, and that understanding better fits contemporary realities than the Sixth Circuit’s payment-focused approach. Given the VPPA’s remedial aim and the real-world privacy harms that fall disproportionately on ordinary users with little bargaining power, I would treat a registered or persistently identified app user as a “subscriber” even if the app is free.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The VPPA defines “consumer” to include not only “renters” and “purchasers,” but also “subscriber[s] of goods or services from a video tape service provider,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1), and nothing in that text requires monetary payment. Read in statutory context, “subscriber” connotes an ongoing relationship (e.g., registration, account-based access, or regular receipt of app-delivered content), but excluding free, app-based video services would create an underinclusive regime that is hard to reconcile with Congress’s privacy-protective design and the modern, ad-supported market in which “payment” often takes the form of data. While Ellis v. Cartoon Network, Inc. cautions against treating every casual viewer as a “subscriber,” it does not justify a payment-focused rule; rather, the workable middle ground is to require some indicia of continuing affiliation beyond passive viewing, which an app download and continued use can supply. This construction preserves administrable limits (not every website visitor is covered) while giving coherent effect to Congress’s choice of “subscriber” alongside “renter” and “purchaser” in § 2710(a)(1).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The VPPA defines a “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1). Read in its 1988 ordinary-public meaning and in the company it keeps, “subscriber” denotes an ongoing, committed relationship—typically involving enrollment for continuing delivery—rather than the one-step download and casual use of a free app, which would collapse the statute’s limiting triad (renter/purchaser/subscriber) into mere viewership. That reading aligns with Ellis v. Cartoon Network, Inc. (11th Cir.), which rejected treating a free-app downloader as a “subscriber” absent a more durable, account-based commitment, and it avoids expanding liability beyond what Congress specified in § 2710(a)(1) and the parallel “rental, sale, or delivery” framing in § 2710(a)(4). Where Congress imposed civil liability with statutory damages, any genuine ambiguity should be resolved narrowly rather than by judicial enlargement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the VPPA, a “consumer” is a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1). Reading “subscriber” in line with its ordinary 1988 meaning and the statute’s focus on renting/purchasing, merely downloading and casually using a free app without any ongoing, committed relationship or registration is insufficient; otherwise the Act would effectively cover any viewer, a result Congress did not adopt when it amended the VPPA’s consent provisions in 2012 without expanding “consumer.” Ellis v. Cartoon Network supplies a workable limiting principle—requiring something more than free access—to avoid sweeping in routine online video viewing and creating impractical, legitimacy-threatening litigation exposure untethered from the statute’s text and history. Respecting precedent and administrable limits, I would affirm that Salazar is not a “consumer” on these facts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under the VPPA’s text, a “consumer” is a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1). Read in context, “subscriber” connotes an ongoing, committed relationship for goods or services—not mere access to freely available content—an understanding reflected in Ellis v. Cartoon Network, Inc., 803 F.3d 1251, 1256–57 (11th Cir. 2015), which emphasized that Congress did not use broader terms like “user” or “viewer” and did not expand “consumer” when amending the Act. Treating every free app download as a “subscription” would stretch “subscriber” beyond its ordinary public meaning and risk converting casual viewing into VPPA coverage untethered to the statute’s purchase/rental/subscription framework. Given that Salazar alleges only free app use without indicia of an ongoing subscriber relationship, he does not plausibly qualify as a “consumer” under § 2710(a)(1).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2710(a)(1) defines a “consumer” to include a “subscriber” of a video tape service provider’s goods or services, and nothing in the text imposes a payment requirement; reading “subscriber” to categorically exclude users of free, account-based apps risks collapsing the statutory term into “renter” or “purchaser” and undermining the VPPA’s privacy-protective purpose. As the First Circuit explained in Yershov v. Gannett, a mobile-app user can plausibly be a “consumer” where the user obtains ongoing access to the provider’s audiovisual materials through the app and supplies something of value in exchange (e.g., personal/device data), even absent money changing hands. That approach also accords with a practical, administrable focus on whether the user has a continuing relationship with the service (not merely a one-off webpage visit), which avoids both an unduly narrow, payment-focused rule and an unbounded expansion to truly casual viewers. Because a modern ad-supported app economy commonly monetizes users through data rather than fees, interpreting “subscriber” to cover such app users better effectuates Congress’s aim to prevent disclosure of individuals’ video-viewing choices under § 2710(b).
